title: The Kiss That Lifted Me
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 8 of 40
content:
For three weeks after dinner, nobody kissed anybody new.

This was, I learned, entirely intentional.

Katara called it giving everyone room.

Aang called it taking things slowly.

Toph called it “the dumbest group decision we’ve ever made,” which was interesting because she had voted for it.

The result was unbearable.

Aang started finding excuses to stand close to me.

Katara’s hand lingered at my back when she passed behind my chair.

Toph became even more shameless about announcing my pulse.

I started spending unreasonable amounts of time thinking about mouths.

The breaking point came at a community feast.

Cranefish Town had completed the eastern footbridge and the council, desperate for good publicity, decided this deserved lanterns, speeches, food stalls, and a stage. I had been assigned to verify vendor permits. Aang had been assigned to give a speech.

Toph had assigned herself to stealing dumplings.

Katara found me near the river just before sunset.

“You look like you’re planning an escape.”

“I am calculating whether anyone would notice if I fell in.”

“I would.”

Her answer was immediate.

I looked at her.

Katara’s smile was soft but not shy.

“Also,” she added, “Toph would complain about having to fish you out.”

“I thought water was your department.”

“She’d complain anyway.”

We walked toward the lanterns together.

The feast was loud, crowded, and beautiful. Earth Kingdom drums answered Fire Nation strings. Children ran across the new bridge with paper lanterns. An old woman sold seaweed buns beside a man grilling spicy peppers. Someone had hung four colors of ribbon from every railing.

Aang took the stage.

His speech lasted four minutes.

This was a miracle.

He talked about bridges being useful because they did not erase the river. They acknowledged distance and made crossing possible.

It was a very Aang metaphor.

It also worked.

When he finished, the crowd applauded. His eyes found us almost immediately.

Katara raised one hand.

Toph, beside her, shouted, “Too long!”

Aang laughed from the stage.

Later, after the official part ended, musicians took over.

Aang loved dancing.

This was less a hobby than a physical law.

He pulled Katara into the crowd first. She protested for exactly ten seconds before laughing and following his lead. Their movements had the ease of people who had danced badly together often enough to become good at it.

Toph stood beside me with her arms folded.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were about to ask if I dance.”

“Do you?”

“No.”

A beat.

“Unless there’s stomping.”

“Convenient.”

The next song had heavy drums.

Toph grabbed my wrist.

I barely had time to laugh before she dragged me into the crowd.

Toph did not dance like Katara.

She fought the music.

Every beat became something to hit with her heel. She moved with sharp confidence, reading the floor through dozens of feet. I stopped trying to follow and let myself answer instead.

When I missed a step, she grinned.

When I recovered, she grinned wider.

Aang and Katara joined us.

For one song, the four of us moved in a loose circle beneath the lanterns.

Nobody belonged to anybody.

Nobody was left out.

It was only dancing.

It felt like practice for something larger.

Then Aang stole me.

He spun between Toph and me, caught my hand, and pulled me toward the edge of the crowd.

“Thief!” Toph yelled.

“You can have them back!” Aang called.

“That is not how this works,” Katara shouted, laughing.

Aang looked at me. “Is that okay?”

The question, asked even in play, mattered.

“Yes.”

He smiled.

We danced badly.

Aang tried to teach me an Air Nomad step involving more hopping than dignity. I stepped on his foot. He nearly backed into a lantern pole. By the end of the song we were laughing too hard to continue.

We escaped to the grass beyond the lights.

The river moved dark beside us.

Music carried from the feast, softened by distance.

Aang sat cross-legged.

I sat beside him.

For a moment neither of us spoke.

Then he said, “I’ve been trying very hard not to kiss you.”

My entire body went still.

“That is a terrible opening line.”

“I know.”

“You’re supposed to be wise.”

“I’m twenty-one.”

“That is the wisest thing you’ve said tonight.”

He laughed.

Then his expression changed.

“I mean it, though.”

“I know.”

“I don’t want to rush you because we had one conversation.”

“I know.”

“I also don’t want taking it slow to become pretending I don’t want things.”

The honesty in his face made my chest ache.

“What do you want?” I asked.

Aang’s eyes lowered to my mouth.

“You know.”

“Say it.”

He swallowed.

“I want to kiss you.”

The world narrowed.

Not because he was the Avatar.

Not because air moved when he breathed.

Because he had asked.

Because he was waiting.

I leaned closer.

“Yes.”

Aang’s hand lifted slowly to my jaw.

His palm was warm.

The first touch of his mouth was gentle.

Almost careful.

Then I smiled against him, and he did too, and whatever nervousness had been keeping us polite broke apart.

The kiss deepened.

Not desperate the way I had once imagined it might be. Hungry, yes, but full of laughter we were both trying not to ruin. His thumb brushed my cheek. My hand caught the front of his robe. He made a soft sound that sent warmth through me from throat to stomach.

Then the grass disappeared.

My eyes opened.

We were floating.

Only a foot above the ground, but definitely floating.

“Aang.”

His eyes opened too.

“Oh.”

“Are you doing this?”

“Not on purpose.”

I started laughing.

That made him laugh.

The air current wobble became worse.

“Aang.”

“I know, I know.”

We drifted sideways.

I grabbed his shoulders.

He wrapped both arms around me.

We landed in a heap.

For several seconds neither of us could breathe from laughing.

From somewhere behind us came Toph’s voice.

“Called it.”

We both froze.

Katara said, “You said you weren’t listening.”

“I wasn’t. They floated.”

I covered my face.

Aang called, “How long have you been there?”

“Long enough,” Toph said.

“Not that long,” Katara added quickly.

I sat up.

They were standing near the lantern line.

Katara’s expression held amusement, tenderness, and something else I could not read.

I stood.

The old reflex to feel guilty rose before I could stop it.

Katara crossed the distance between us.

She touched my arm.

“Hey.”

I looked at her.

“You don’t have to look sorry.”

“I’m not.”

Toph snorted.

I sighed. “Fine. I was for half a second.”

Katara’s fingers tightened gently around my arm.

“Aang kissing you doesn’t take anything from me.”

Aang came up beside us. “And Katara loving you wouldn’t take anything from me.”

Toph folded her arms. “And if anybody starts keeping score, I’m eating the scorecard.”

I laughed.

Katara’s gaze moved to my mouth again.

My pulse jumped.

Toph groaned. “Oh, spirits. Here we go.”

Katara smiled.

“Not tonight,” she said, though she did not look away.

The anticipation in those two words was almost worse than a kiss.

Aang slipped his fingers through mine.

Katara took my other hand.

Toph complained that hand-holding was structurally inefficient, then hooked two fingers into the back of my sleeve as we walked toward the feast.

The lanterns glowed over the bridge.

Music rose.

My lips still tingled.

For once, I did not ask myself what any of it meant.

I already knew enough.

I had been kissed.

I had been caught.

And when the ground disappeared, three people had been waiting for me to come back down.

The next morning, Aang apologized for lifting me off the ground.

This was complicated by the fact that I had enjoyed it.

We sat on the back steps while Katara argued with a laundry line and Toph loudly claimed not to be listening from the courtyard.

“I should have asked,” Aang said.

“You were kissing me.”

“That is not the same as permission to airbend you.”

The seriousness in his voice made me stop trying to rescue him from the discomfort.

“No,” I said. “It isn’t.”

He nodded once.

“I wasn’t frightened after I realized what was happening,” I added. “But I was surprised.”

“I felt happy and my bending just—” He made a helpless motion with both hands. “That’s not an excuse.”

“No.”

Another nod.

Then I smiled. “It was also extremely dramatic.”

His ears turned red.

From the yard, Toph shouted, “It was ridiculous!”

“You said you weren’t listening,” Aang called.

“I lied.”

Katara emerged carrying a basket of wet clothes. “For what it’s worth, you two floating three feet off the ground while Toph screamed commentary was not the romantic masterpiece either of you thinks it was.”

“I think it was a masterpiece,” I said.

Aang looked at me hopefully.

“A terrible one.”

He laughed, relief loosening his shoulders.

Then he offered his hand palm-up between us.

“Can I?”

I placed mine in it.

“Yes.”

A breeze curled around our joined fingers—small, controlled, no stronger than the air through an open window.

This time I felt it before it moved.

This time I chose to stay inside it.
